Because of using the city_id we were not getting full data and it seemed like a gap.

Thus this order has all of its data in both Presto and Protobuf S3, no gap.

We also had a testing branch in Spark to help us decode data from both protobuf and Presto ([https://github.com/bolteu/spark/pull/1649|https://github.com/bolteu/spark/pull/1649|smart-link]) and we did not find any gaps for multiple days.

Additionally, we added one more exception catching in order to not miss any other possible failure while processing data. [https://github.com/bolteu/spark/pull/1643/files|https://github.com/bolteu/spark/pull/1643/files]

This can be closed, no gaps found.

*Issue with Amex*

* Amex reports are formatted with their own proprietary file format GRRCN (global reconcilliation). They provide a [Perl package|https://metacpan.org/pod/Finance::AMEX::Transaction] for parsing, but AFAIK it’s not available in python. Need to investigate the file parser script.
* Amex reports only available in the SFTP server for a short time. All files are stored under {{outbox}} folder, until the file is downloaded. Once the file is downloaded, the file is moved to {{sent}} folder. This mechanism complicates the data ingestion! 😞 
* [Python package|https://github.com/lumoslabs/pyxmex/tree/master] for AMEX parser, but still doesn’t support GRRCN filetype. Maybe we could fork this repo and add a new parser type for GRRCN. The technical guide for GRRCN is here → [https://drive.google.com/file/d/1V4l6QOjmpoHqKOQBSLBTM2LXgOwFe1l5/view|https://drive.google.com/file/d/1V4l6QOjmpoHqKOQBSLBTM2LXgOwFe1l5/view|smart-link] 
* In the meantime, we’re asking Amex to also provide CSV data, as in their [webpage|https://www.americanexpress.com/us/merchant/raw-data.html] they state that they support it.

Hi!

Feedback after today's meeting with *Consumer Protection (ANPC)* - Mrs Stirbu. 

She more or less understands our limits when it comes to GDPR, although she disagrees with our restrictions when the requests come from a public authority. I explained that Data Protection agencies expect Bolt to be responsible when sharing data, including with the authorities, if the respective data may involve other people.

They also agree that such complaints have nothing to do with ANPC, however they are obliged to analyse and solve these tickets. And they can't solve them if they don't have info from us.

*For example, the two tickets above*:

* The plaintiffs sent account statements to ANPC and claim that out of x rides they only went with y rides. We both agreed that we cannot share data about other people, who are not related to the complainant's account. 
* Therefore, she needs from us the invoices that strictly belong to the claimants' account (October - up to the date when the claim was made). If the invoices prove that out of 10 trips, only 5 were made by the plaintiffs, then ANPC will advise them to go to the Police if they consider that a fraud was committed.
* Also, Bolt can notify ANPC that it is blocking the respective card if the claimant expressly requests it.

*Regarding the ticket from Aura Mega* - fyi [~accountid:61268a40129802006ae93f05]

After an investigation with [~accountid:6102799ceb7aef0069a1f5e4], we concluded that the most likely reason why the execution time is so long for some orders is due to the transaction locking state log rows in the endpoints moving states. Those transactions are kept for a while, making multiple DB queries. During that time, we can not fetch state logs. This affects active orders.

Since the number of affected orders are relatively small, and since the cause of this problem is deeply rooted in the move state mechanism, we thought that we can live with this elevated latency until we get complaints from clients.

Possible solutions we explored, to circumvent this problem without redesigning the move state logic were:

* Fetching only unlocked state logs
* Fetching locked state logs with their values before the transaction was open

We weren’t happy with either of those.

*Note for file from CC:*

* The CCPC is the local regulator in Ireland. 
* They told us last year that we have regulatory obligations to report complaints online. 
* Initially I was told this was a Product Legal issue - given it would also apply to EU countries. 
* Julius informed me on a call that it is instead a local Irish problem, but once we develop a solution on reporting then we can roll it out in other EU countries. 
* Basically, we are obligated to publish complaints (volume etc) online annually - but there is limited information on how this information needs to be ‘published’ and how this should be presented online publicly.
* When we made inquiries with the regulator (CCPC) they didnt give us much intel and didnt give us the examples we requested for how to present this information, their sentiment basically was ‘figure it out yourself’. 
* So, last year we provided this information to the CCPC to be compliant as possible, however, we still need to determine a good system of practice here. 

*Next steps:* 

* Look at what this regulation requires. 
* Look at what competitors do with respect to reporting. 
* Map out how this ideally should look online, for how long we should hold it online (perhaps permanently) and what information is required. It is likely we will get approached soon by the CCPC, so best to determine a way forward now. 
* Once known, we can consult with the CCPC and Irish team to roll out the solution.

Hey! Thanks for raising this. 

In general, if no personal data of the rider is recorded (no facial image, no voice), then data protection issues would not come into play. How do you see that it could disclose the rider pickup and destination? 

However, if any personal data should be processed (there is a facial image, you hear the voice etc), then as you referred filming may be fine from the privacy standpoint but there are several rules that need to be followed (having a proper legal basis, providing the data subject information about the processing, deleting data, only collecting as much data as needed etc). These rules in such cases need to be followed by the driver since he will be acting as the controller of the data. If Bolt would not have any type of access to these recordings, then we would not be liable per privacy regulations.

In conclusion, since there may be a risk that personal data will also be fetched (eg. the rider is talking), then privacy rules apply and the driver should be doing this in a compliant manner. As Bolt is probably notified of such activities by the riders, then it would be good to reach out to the drivers and educate them on the legality of such filming but we would not be compelled to do this.

Thanks for raising this. From privacy standpoint, if any personal data is exchanged with a supplier, then a contract should be put in place depending on the roles of the parties (who is processing the data and how). This assessment can be done by the privacy team (or [~accountid:63da287e790148a18093a774] can also help with first assessments). 

Additional to having in place the agreement with the company, we also need a legal basis for exchanging this data that would also be communicated to the data subject (this case driver). Usually the legal basis for such data sharing is consent or legitimate interest. That will also be assessed by the privacy team. 

Besides the contract and legal basis, there are several other principles that need to be kept in mind such as only collecting as much data as necessary, deleting data, putting in place proper access controls etc. But here again, most certain would be to create a ticket to us or legal counsel (who will also loop us in) in order to have the privacy compliance checked.

h4.  *🚗 🛴 What if the user cannot reserve a vehicle/order a trip due to negative Bolt Balance?*

If the user has negative Bolt Balance, they're unable to see it when they've travelled to another country. Due to this, they're also unable to top-up their balance to clear the debt.

If that's the case, follow these steps:

* Check which trip has caused negative Bolt Balance
** Go to the user's transaction history and look for _Booking_ that has 💳 _failed_ and 🟢 _success_ (see the screenshot below). This means the card payment was failed, but we've successfully charged everything to Bolt Balance. 
* Open the ride connected to this transaction and *refund it fully to the user's Bolt Balance*
* Advise the user to try to place an order again

h2. Fw: BOLT Riders Team


**

Hello Team, 
Thank you for your time and open discussion today.
Below you will find an overview and some technical details about the solution.
*GOAL: Using website event conversion optimisation to drive in-app events. Helping overcome SKAN difficulties.*
*There are two types of mWEB (web2app) for APP clients:*
* Using payment on the web
* Utilizing redirect to AppStore / Google Play
*This guide aims to uncover the second one.*

*ARE THERE ANY LIMITATIONS?*
*"Redirect" uses deeplinks to pass Facebook Pixel parameters (e.g. OneLink by AppsFlyer). Deeplinks are not supported by Apple for iOS 14.5+, so signals from this traffic cannot be attributed.*
*To highlight: the Pre-Landing Solution drops up to 90% of events.*

*HOW IT WORKS*
*The Pre-Landing Solution helps converting and attributing mobile website visitors into mobile app users utilising deeplinks to pass FB Pixel parameters to the back-end, match them with in-app events and push back into Pixel using Conversions API.*
*Landing Page*
*Users arrive at a website before reaching your app store page, after engaging with advertising campaigns. The page contains deeplinks from the web page to the app store.*
*The deeplink script (*[*OneLink Smart Script*|https://support.appsflyer.com/hc/en-us/articles/360000677217-OneLink-Smart-Script-Web-to-app-URL-generator]*) dynamically generate unique outgoing OneLink long URLs leading to the app store which contains parameters:*
* *FBP*
* *FBC*
* *User Agent*
* *Client IP address*
* *etc.*
*Example:*
[*https://websiteURL.com/sS7F?pid=onepage_landing&c=store_full&amp*|https://websiteurl.com/sS7F?pid=onepage_landing&c=store_full&amp]*;*
*deep_link_value=onepage_landing&*
*deep_link_sub1=client_ip_address XXXXXXXXX*
*client_user_agent%3DMozilla%2F5.0%20(Macintosh%3B%20Intel%20Mac%20OS%20X%2010_15_7)%20AppleWebKit%2F537.36%20(KHTML%2C%20like%20Gecko)%20Chrome%2F92.0.4515.131%20Safari%2F537.36%26*
*fbp%3Dfb.1.1628757889326.fb.1.1628666022146.483530253%26*
*fbc%3Dfb.1.1628757889326.IwAR3zVgTsuRHmKc2WPlKxJUpnxXAV29XzeZ5R3GboRagrV65ZPUNq2CwyYbw*
*The detailed guide of attribution structure and link parameters used by AppsFlyer is* [*here*|https://support.appsflyer.com/hc/en-us/articles/207447163-Attribution-link-structure-and-parameters]*.*
*The Pixel Data and website events are being pushed to the back-end for further matching either.*

*AppStore*
*The user installs the app using a standard Appstore functionality, passes the app onboarding with further in-app events. The events sends to back-end with the deeplink ID (OneLink ID).*

*Back-End*
*There are two touch points: website events data and in-app events data which could be matched using deeplink ID. The matched events sends to the Pixel by server to server integration (CAPI) using four parameters mentioned above.*

*Issue:* Unnecessary escalations to Tier 2 / local OPS

*Missing instructions:* Tier 1 agents can check the Huru background check results (driver profile > _Documents_ tab > click _View_ for the Huru background check):

* if the result is *clear* or *positive*, Tier 1 can unblock the user;
* if the result is *hit*, the driver can’t be unblocked, and CS should escalate to the local OPS

*User voice:* 

* [case|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/213615451] - “I need to upload my CRC check, how can I do it” (user was unsure how to get to the driver portal, case got escalated to Tier 2)
* [case|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/218716259] - “my account is blocked even though I provided documents”
* [case|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/218698663] - “my account is blocked even though my documents were approved”

*There are three parts to this request:*

* Determining in which article to implement the instructions for checking the Huru background check results and unblocking the driver if possible;
* Drivers providing documents via CS inquiries (in-app, email):
** There was a case when the driver seemed to be unaware about the Driver Portal. If it’s a newly registered driver that got his account approved, but we blocked it due to missing or incorrect documents, is it possible that during this time we may not have informed them of the Driver Portal yet?
** Is it possible that driver leads in South Africa may get approved before all documents are checked, and then their account blocked due to issues with some documents? 
** If the driver’s account is blocked, can they upload documents in the Driver Portal?
** Should we even review documents drivers send via in-app or email - or is it best to ask the driver to upload the document via the Driver Portal and delete the document from the case?
* Drivers being confused why their account was blocked even though they provided all required documents:
** Based on the user voice in all the above examples, it looks like some drivers get approved even before all their documents are reviewed. When the document review is finished, the driver’s account may get blocked. Could it be that the communication of the reason why their account is blocked is less clear/transparent than when their driver application is rejected?

In principle there are no restrictions regarding campaigns or advertising in the form described in the main ticket.

Nonetheless, there are several topics which need to be considered in relation to this type of campaigns, as follows:

* it is necessary to obtain the fleet's consent before offering this type of campaign to their employees.
** There is judicial practice in Romania where this type of incentive offered to the employees of a partner without the approval of the employer was deemed as bribery. 
** The rationale behind this is that the end goal of the incentive may conflict with the fleet's commercial interest (e.g. the fleet's commercial strategy may be to focus their efforts on another platform), and this direct relation with their employees bypasses the employer.
** This should be relevant for both KPI campaigns and advertising, therefore a contract signed with the fleet specifying the terms of the campaign and payments made to the fleet are advisable.
* from a competition perspective, in relation to KPI campaigns, Bolt should check if it may be deemed to hold a dominant position in one of the cities where the campaign is available (a 40% market share is an indicator for dominance). 
** Incentives applied by dominant undertakings have been found abusive when given in exchange for customer loyalty or when they are found to be loyalty-inducing. 
** For instance, incentives which are likely to induce exclusivity are likely to be considered an abuse of dominant position, if Bolt were to hold such position (see Case T-286/09 _Intel v Commission_ ECLI:EU:T:2014:54).
** This should be relevant for KPI campaigns, but not for pure advertising. 
* Specific to advertising, certain municipalities have raised a claim under Law no. 185/2013 on the location and authorisation of advertising media, which provides an authorization procedure for vehicle advertisement. 
** This legislation, reasonably, does not apply to brand stickers on cars, but to vehicles which impede traffic (e.g. with oversize billboards, loud music, etc.), and we have managed to successfully push back against such claims, however we may not exclude that they will occur in the future, as well.

Let us know if you need further details on the above.

*PL*

PL Ops team obtained a PL specific tax interpretation (tax team should know more details) concerning netting commission mechanism which is of importance for Bolt branding agreements in PL. Generally (summary from Joanna Groszfeld):

* We now use a netting mechanism on our commission invoice - that is, commission is reduced by the value of the bonuses we pay to our fleets and drivers.
* in order to apply this mechanism, we received a tax interpretation from the Ministry of Finance, and this interpretation states that only bonuses that are given to drivers for transport services rendered can reduce commission; marketing bonuses are not included. 
* We are defending ourselves with branding by saying that we do in fact pay a bonus for the ride driven, but only to branded cars. 
* For these reasons, we have to avoid saying that it is a "marketing bonus", because the separate invoice for marketing services may be required.

The above issue has been considered in the current template of PL branding agreement available [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Zr-drpwfR9teaRzIOSumtHrb1ykZHLGJ/edit#]. 

Otherwise, no any additional constraints that would block Bolt from implementing both models. Some additional thoughts from the external below:

* The campaign settlement model itself as well as advertising is in our view acceptable. From a civil law point of view, the billing rules should be regulated precisely enough so that there are no disputes with individual drivers / fleet companies regarding the calculation of remuneration/bonus.
* Restrictions on placing advertisements on cars (Road Transport Act Article 18(5) - but this only applies to occasional carriage - and such is prohibited by the Bolt Regulations).
* Some leasing companies in the OWL prohibit the wrapping of cars with advertisements or require additional approval.
* Parking a car covered with advertising is permitted. Occupying a road lane by a car with an advertisement (so-called "advertising poles") without the permission of the road manager - no longer.
* The Traffic Law and the Ordinance on Technical Requirements for Vehicles implicitly prohibit the placing of visibility-restricting stickers.

For completeness, adding the additional comments from the external counsel:

* The Romanian Criminal Code has adopted the common law approach on the criminal liabilities of legal entities, meaning that no criminal offences are _de plano_ excluded from the liability of legal entities. Practice has formed around criminal offences related to tax evasion, employment and other corporate offences, but, nonetheless, IP infringement or accessing an IT system without authorization are not excluded from triggering corporate liability.
* Legal entities are liable for criminal offenses perpetrated while carrying out their main activity or when acting in the interest or on behalf of the legal person. Any person acting on behalf of the legal entity may trigger its liability (from top management to employees or even third parties), but in practice, it is necessary that the criminal activity is approved or at least well known by the management of the legal entity (since these criminal offences are formally conditioned upon the intentional behaviour of the perpetrator). 
* Investigators usually jointly pursue both the company and the individual(s) which took part in the offense, since there are higher chances of recovering damages.
* As regards the sanctions, the Romanian Criminal Code provides a rather complicated system of calculating criminal fines, also leaving a great degree of freedom to the court (similar to imprisonment for individuals). In relation to the criminal offences identified in the questionnaire, the fines would range from RON 100 to RON 1,200,000 (approx. EUR 25 to EUR 240,000).

# specific requirements on refunds - I have looked into this online and found the following information: 

*Relevant Legislation* - [Consumer Protection Act (Finnish)|https://www.finlex.fi/fi/laki/ajantasa/1978/19780038#L8P12] 

* Compensation for a defect in a service can take the form of rectifying the defect and redoing the work (this is not possible in the scenario above), a price reduction or cancellation of the contract. If rectifying the defect or redoing the work is not possible, or the company does not rectify the defect within a reasonable time, the customer may demand a price reduction.

+*Defects in Taxi Services*+

The company is responsible for a defect in a taxi service if:

* the content, performance or results of the service do not correspond to what can be deemed to have been agreed.  For example, the taxi arrives at a different time than what you agreed, it does not arrive at all, or its equipment deviates from what you agreed; 
* the service was not provided professionally and with care, the passenger’s interests were not taken into account, including the needs of a passenger with restricted functional capacity, or the driver has chosen a route that is not appropriate for the passenger; 
* the service does not meet the ordinary expectations of passengers concerning taxi services; 
* the service does not match the information provided in connection with marketing and it can be expected that the information affected the consumer’s decision, or the company did not provide some information that the customer could justifiably have expected to receive; and 
* the service does not meet the requirements laid down in an act, decree or authority’ decision.

+*Price re­duc­tion*+

* You can usually demand a price reduction if the taxi service is defective because such methods as rectifying the defect or re-performing the service may not be possible in the case of taxi services. The price reduction should correspond to the value of the defect.
* If the defect is substantial and cannot be rectified by means of a price reduction, the ultimate remedy is cancelling the contract.

+*Can­celling the con­tract*+

* Cancelling the contract is usually possible in case of a major defect or delay.  The passenger may cancel the contract before or after the journey.

*Note:* You must always have a receipt or other reliable information on the costs. No compensation is provided for distress, mental suffering or loss of free time.

Hi [~accountid:62bbfa39ec4c0d377f9fc3b7] I have looked into the above query online (google, practical law and LexisNexis) to try and locate a practice guidance note on the exact position under Finnish law. Unfortunately, I have not found a definitive answer to the question asked on the ticket. A lot of the information that I am sourcing online is in relation to defective goods or services (but not services in the context of ride hailing apps). Any of the information I am locating  online addressing the law on refunds and credit notes but does not specifically answer the question asked on this ticket.  

See below a summary of some of the information I have found: 

*Further research notes:* 

Website sources: [EU Website |https://europa.eu/youreurope/citizens/consumers/shopping/guarantees-returns/index_en.htm],  [https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/consumer/changed-your-mind/cancelling-a-service-youve-arranged/|https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/consumer/changed-your-mind/cancelling-a-service-youve-arranged/|smart-link] ,  [https://www.citizensinformation.ie/en/consumer/consumer-laws/your-consumer-rights/|https://www.citizensinformation.ie/en/consumer/consumer-laws/your-consumer-rights/|smart-link] . Practical Law and Lexix Nexis. 

*Faulty goods:* under EU rules, a trader must repair, replace, reduce the price or give you a refund if goods you bought turn out to be faulty or do not look or work as advertised -{color:#ff5630} This is not applicable to the scenario above as being charged for ‘paid wait time’ does not fall under the category of faulty goods. {color}

*Purchasing a product or a service online:* 14 day cooling off period rule. In the EU you have the right to return purchases made online or through other types of distance selling, such as by phone, mail order or from a door-to-door salesperson, within 14 days for a full refund. You can do so for any reason – even if you simply changed your mind.

The 14-day cooling off period +does not apply to all purchases+. Some of the exemptions are:

* plane and train tickets, as well as concert tickets, hotel bookings, car rental reservations and catering services for specific dates. - {color:#ff5630}Would ride hailing fall within this category? if so, then the 14 day cooling off period is not applicable. {color}
* goods and drinks delivered to you by regular delivery – for example delivery by a milkman
* goods made to order or clearly personalised – such as a tailor-made suit
* sealed audio, video or computer software, such as DVDs, which you have unsealed upon receipt
* online digital content, if you have already started downloading or streaming it and you agreed that you would lose your right of withdrawal by starting the performance
* goods bought from a private individual rather than a company/trader
* urgent repairs and maintenance contracts – if you call a plumber to repair a leaking shower, you can't cancel the work once you have agreed on the price of the service

Please note that this list is not exhaustive.

The cooling off period expires 14 days after the day you received your goods. For service contracts, the cooling off period expires 14 days after the day you concluded the contract. If the cooling off period expires on a non-working day, your deadline is extended till the next working day.

In regards to goods businesses are legally allowed to offer a credit note instead of a full refund (in certain circumstances such as when a consumer changes their mind on the purchase, but the goods are not defective) although there are some circumstances where this does not apply and consumers are legally entitled to a full refund as opposed to a credit note or voucher. See below when the credit note rule does not apply:  

# Items or services bought online which you cancel or return during the ‘cooling off period’ - not applicable in this situation
# Flight cancellations and package holiday cancellations - not applicable in this situation 

I do not think the above research addresses the question asked as ride hailing would not fall under the category of *‘goods’* and it is not clear if it would fall under ‘*Purchasing a product or a service online’.* If it does fall within the category of ‘Purchasing a product or a service online’ it is unlikely that the  14 day cooling off period would be applicable after reviewing the exemptions to this rule. 

+*To Summarise*+

Under the laws in the UK you have to give the consumer a choice between a refund to the payment method that was originally used or alternatively a credit note/gift voucher, businesses are not entitled to refund by only credit note/voucher (in this instance refunding back to Bolt Balance) as this would result in a breach of consumer regulations. Under UK law consumers are entitled to insist on a full refund in the same way that payment was originally made.
